chapters.title: Part I
epi: There is an old illusion. It is called good and evil.

chapters.label: Chapter 1
chapters.title: An Unsettling Premise

paras.d: Title: An Autobiography of God: Unveiling Reality, Diluting Religion, and Quantifying Faith. Ph.D. Thesis

paras: “Allow me to ponder this deeply profound query—our perception of the existence of God. If traditional philosophies fail to provide insight, must we not question not the existence of God but the manner of it? Not the why, but how? May I then challenge your perceptions by posing a provocatively unsettling hypothesis?

If the belief that “the day of our deaths is predetermined” is held, it may lead us to accept the fate of suicide in cases of suicide victims. This view suggests that the act of suicide is not a choice made by the individual but rather a predetermined fate.
In other causes of death, reasons need to exist as to the instant and instance of a person's death. Now, consider this:
What if the whole world were to unanimously die by suicide?

If every person were to simultaneously and voluntarily take their lives through methods such as wrist-slitting, hanging, or shooting themselves in the head, would it suggest that this mass suicide was predetermined by God?
If the answer is no, then deduction begs one to conclude that there is no predetermined instant for dying and that not all deaths are sanctioned by God. This hypothesis yields several results:
That mankind, to a reasonable extent, is in control of its fate.
That men are at liberty to live and die however and whenever they please.
The rest do not matter in the context of our conversation. But the conclusion is that:
There is no predetermination to our lives except for divine providence. Therefore, free will exists, and we are in complete control.
Mankind's existence is like a brick mansion built on hay; the only thing holding us together is faith.

I do not lay claim to the ownership of this thought or the ideas it develops in your mind. However, I would like to think that you are an intelligent human capable of questioning and countering your speculations. This narration is intended as an argument against yourself. Think of it as a zero-sum game. I make my move, and if it pleases you, you make yours by agreeing to my inferences, wherever they may lead, or better yet, play against me and carve your path. After all, it is common wisdom that the journey to enlightenment is steep and dangerous, and we do not get far by thinking only those thoughts that make us comfortable.

For an objective analysis of the universe, our tool of measurement will be intelligence. Long, have many wondered about the concept of intelligence. What makes one intelligent? Wisdom, we easily understand. That is a trait reserved for those who have the humility to apply knowledge only when it is severely demanded. Like trickles of water, wise men hold on to their wisdom to diffuse it only when it may be useful. But intelligence, as we have seen, unlike wisdom, can be a catalyst for good and evil. No wise man can be deemed evil, for wisdom is not synonymous with being a villain. Knowledge, however, is an open interface that fuses with whoever has the capacity to wield its power. We do not ask what power is. This is not a matter of philosophy but of logic. If faith can be deemed logical, that is. Yet, although there might be no logic to faith, we cannot contend that there is reason, and that, an abundance of it.

So, what is reason? And why does it exist? That, too, would be treading down a false path. For, asking the obvious only leads to obvious destinations. We already possess reason, so asking why would be born of hubris or a wanton waste of boredom. But how does reason exist? Does this not sound refreshing? Are you not forced to relish the fact that this line of questioning opens up simultaneous and contradictory thought patterns? There goes my point, if you have been paying attention. This hypothesis is not about asking why or knowing when to ask how. It’s about asking. Why do we even have to ask? And if we dare, how? The goal is in the questioning.

Why does God do what he does? No, that doesn’t sound good enough to be the basis of our thesis. The interest is in how He does it. Or, have you not understood? That by the highest form of asking, you elicit the highest order of answers. Why would God want to die for humanity, most ask, concerning salvation? The answer is a simple summary of the word “love.” But how does He intend to do it? Do you really agree that God’s means of showing that He loves us justifies the end? After all, if God is willing to let so many of us die, does He really love us for who we are as individuals, or does He love us as a collective? Does He accept what we accept and love us from our own perspective of what love means to us? Or does He love otherwise, granting us love from His perspective of what love means to Him?

If I were to jump down a ledge and, in so doing, tempt the Lord our God, who has promised to give his angels charge over me, would I die or would I survive? Whichever one it is, would it have been the hand of God at work? If it goes well and I meet my end, was that God's intention, or did I choose my fate? If it goes amiss and I am saved, thus violating my own free will so I can exist to serve a greater purpose and die when it pleases Him, would we believe in miracles and acknowledge God's hand at play? And if we do, has He not taken away my choice, forcing me to remain alive to His own end?

This thesis is an experiential paper on the quality of human lives and how our existence as a species is influenced by our belief in or disbelief in God. Although the paper failed to quantitatively accurately assess and demystify the existence of God, it did prove that there is indeed a devil and that cosmic forces that are at play are influenced by humanity’s actions.
The following narrative is a series of events that happened during the course of my research that significantly impacted the qualitative outcome.”
Maximus took a deep breath and stared at the uninterested audience.
“This story began when someone decided to cross a line…”

chapters.label: Chapter 2
chapters.title: The Hand of God
paras: "Who will entice Ahab, that he may go up and die at Ramoth-Gilead?"

More killing. Do they not get tired of fighting? All they crave is war and disorganization. All they desire is chaos. Yet, I would not blame them. I have chosen not to interfere with the devil’s activities. Still, it is sad.

He sighed. The court remained silent. He could have given a command, but He asked their opinion before taking action. It wasn’t like He didn’t know the right course to take. He had laid down rules, and He followed them as an example for them to follow.

They looked around, everyone at their neighbor. Zehra kept silent too, having recently returned from Israel, where he went to have fun. Most eyes diverted to him and shifted away. He was considered rebellious, but the rules did not forbid him from using his talents on these frail humans.

He sighed and walked forward grimly. He carried himself with pride enough to befit someone of heavenly status, yet not enough to deter his humility. He would hate to be cast down. Earth was good enough for play, but he did not wish to live there, and he certainly did not wish to burn. Unlike what most said about the infinite length of eternity, he knew how finite it could be when your days were numbered. Living forever had surely proven not to be boring.
He bowed.

“I will entice him,” Zehra said. He looked down to avoid a direct gaze. It wasn’t that he could even look directly into God’s eyes if he tried. He had felt the cogs of his soul stop the one time that he had attempted that. He had found himself too sober with soul-searching. He preferred his normal, mischievous self.
“By what means will you entice him?”
Zehra swallowed. For a God who knew the future, he sure had a way of testing your every move.
“I will go out and be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.”

The silence was tense. Zehra wondered if he had made the wrong suggestion. He took a step back and started to retreat backward. It was people, humans, God’s most precious creatures. What in the heavens was he thinking?
“You are to entice him, and you shall succeed; go out and do so.”
Zehra bowed and smiled as he left. Yes! Yes! Yes! He now had permission to play.

God watched Zehra leave. It had come to this—manipulation. This was not how it was supposed to be. Had they not learned anything from the time of the flood? What about Sodom and Gomorrah? Nothing? Were people so eager to make mistakes in the name of progress and, in doing so, repeat history? Humanity had become a loop. He missed Samuel, David, and even Solomon. Those had been men who had lived and dared for the right reasons. We will meet again soon, my friends.

Why had he chosen to create man? Why shouldn’t he have? In the beginning, he had felt lonely. He had looked down on the earth and on the water upon it. It had all been water. He smiled. In the future, some scientists will say that humans were born from this water as an evolved species. What would they not do or say? Even now, they had not done their worst. The worst was all the things that they did in his name. They had eaten the fruit from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Humans were capable of the greatest good. The same were capable of the worst evil. Should he wipe them out again, like he did before? To what end? It was the same self-replicating cycle.
Zehra… What was he doing with Micaiah?
“Just a little lie; all the prophets are saying it; no one would notice. The kings would not be any wiser.”
“Yet, the Lord has shown me what is true. Why do you want me to lie?”
“It is the will of God that the king should die. His time has come.”
Micaiah gasped. “But lying to lead him to his death will make me a murderer.”
“One small death for the good of Israel. What is it to you, Micaiah? Is it not God that you serve? Will you now oppose his will?”
“I will do what is right, just, and true.”
“Very well. Stubborn as ever, I see.”
Zehra disappeared just as the door opened and the soldiers came in to present the prophet to the king. He stood beside the king, smiling and dusting his apparel.
“Your majesty.”
“Oh dear!” Zehra mused.
Micaiah composed himself to remain undistracted.
Zehra bowed. “Go on, my loyal, honest subject. Tell me that I shall die today, and I will have your head.”
“Silence,” Micaiah muttered.
The court murmured its disapproval, and Zehra laughed.
“Micaiah, I know your evil intentions, but I will ask nonetheless. Shall we go to Ramoth-Gilead to battle, or shall I refrain?”
Micaiah was tense. “Go up and triumph; they will be given into your hand.”
King Ahab laughed, and the court followed. Zehra was pleased. He laughed and clapped too, resting his hands on the throne as he leaned in on it.

“Micaiah says something good about me. This may very well be my last day.” He finished laughing and went on, “How many times shall I make you swear that you speak to me nothing but the truth in the name of the Lord?”
Micaiah paused as he looked around. Zehra crossed one leg in front of the other and waited in anticipation along with the court.
“I saw all Israel scattered on the mountains…” He began and narrated everything that had gone on in heaven, as he had seen.
“So God showed you why I came? Now my fun has been ruined.” Zehra sighed. “No matter, the king will not change his mind. He is destined to die.”
After listening to him, King Ahab, outraged, commanded that Micaiah be sent to prison until his return.
Micaiah stared at the wall of the dungeon. He was not the first prophet to have been here. He sighed and sat down on the cold floor.

“I told you that his mind was made up,” Zehra said. “Even right now, he is preparing to disguise himself on the battlefield. It is a marvel to behold how an insignificant man like King Ahab conspires to outwit God. He can’t even outthink me.”
“What are you going to do now?” Micaiah asked. “Your task is done.”
“I will roam the earth and try to stay hidden, lest the wrong people see me.” He bowed. “So long, Micaiah.” So saying, he disappeared.

So far as I recall, no one knows my origin. I remember everything, but I do not remember being a child; I do not remember being anything other than what I’d always been. Even though time itself has changed, I am how I have always been. I wanted more than to be. I wanted to experience something other than being who I was. That was why I created man: for community, love, sacrifice, and happiness. I wanted to enjoy the wind and talk while walking on the grass among the trees. I wanted to experience a different kind of love. I wanted something new that would see me as more than God. I wanted to be understood. Humanity was my attempt at divine understanding.

Zehra was in the tavern in his human form. He had ordered some wine and was settling down to the good grapes of Israel, enjoying the tinge of war that was in the air, when another man walked into the tavern. Zehra knew it was trouble. The dark shroud around him thickened as he approached. Although the same scent filled the air in this place, this man smelled like he had bathed in it. It was enticing but dangerous. It was pride, the worst of all sins.
The man sat in front of him and removed his cloak. He was handsome.
“Don’t you get tired of playing on one side, Zehra?”
“I came to do God’s bidding; that is not one-sided play, it is work.” Zehra sipped his drink while trying to keep his insides from churning.
“I have a proposition for you.” The man said.
“We know how your offers go, Son of the Morning.”
The man laughed. It was good-hearted and genuine.
“What if I told you that God intended to come live in this filth as one of them?”
“He cannot.” Zehra set down his drink.
“It is unworthy of the glory of heaven. Not to mention the disgust of our God living among sinners.”
“Our God?”
“He is my creator, Zehra; I owe him my life.” The man said it emphatically.
“What do you need?”
“Centuries from now, a child will be born to a certain family. I want you to make sure that the child is not killed during the massacre that will follow within the year of his birth.”
“I don’t understand. You want me to protect a child? Not just any child, Zehra. His name will be Judas, the son of Iscariot. I want you to make sure that he lives.”
“How will this benefit God?” Zehra asked.
“Do you remember Abram, Moses, Enoch, Elijah, Isaiah, and...”
“Yes, yes, yes, I get the point. Great men who singlehandedly changed the working of things.”
“Yes, Zehra. This child that we will protect is the one who will end this love that blinds our father, which makes him want to come down to this lowly earth because of man.”
“I can’t believe that he would do that. Being born alone would make him susceptible to sin.”
“If God sins, who will rule heaven then?” The man said as he stood up and bowed. Wearing his cloak, he walked out of the tavern and was gone.
“But why, God?” Zehra twirled the drink in his cup.

He heard the horns blowing in the distance. Ahab was dead, the war was over, and his job was done. He took a gulp, and in the commotion that followed the people running to hear the outcome of the battle, he disappeared.
“Will you not do anything about Zehra?” Michael asked.
“Not at all. Everyone has free will, Michael, everyone.”

chapters.label: Chapter 3
chapters.title: The Perspective
paras: "You didn’t tell me that your plan was to kill God," Zehra said solemnly, recalling how he had protected Judas, who would later betray Christ. Christ! He thought. Thank God he had not been punished for it.
"It's not like it served its purpose. In the end, God won."
"I wonder where that leaves me." Zehra contemplated. "You've done well to drag me to your side."
"Do you enjoy their company?" He asked.
Zehra thought for a while before answering. "I like them. Somehow, they make the simplicity of heaven complex. They are more than I expect."
"Yes. They can be interesting." He stood beside him, looking down at the city. "Remember Job?"
Zehra laughed. "He sure beat my expectations. I thought he would crack after his friends caved."
"Yes. I thought the same." He clenched his hands. "I hated that match.” How could a human be so loyal?

"I think there is something about being human that we would never understand. I don't think our father did either. I think that's why he had to become one of them. His creatures are fascinating. And they are the least of us."
"Hmmm." He sighed.

"What would you do now? Your time is running out. I know that apologies have gone off the table. You've run out of grace.""I may as well live, Zehra. All I have is time. Like you said, it's running out."

Zehra looked down solemnly. Sometimes he felt bad for him. They had been close in heaven. During the rebellion, he had thought about joining him, but he had preferred his comfort. He was a diplomat, not a warrior. He had no quarrel with God.
"Who is that?" Zehra pointed at a boy walking out of school.
"I don't know, but angels are watching over him." He smiled. "It seems like that leaves his friends in my hands."
"You have found your fun." Zehra mused. "What will you do?"
"If you stay, you may be entertained. What are a few years to you?"
"I could stay. After all, compared to you, I have all the time in all the worlds."
"Haha."

Sad, Zehra thought. They could not see him. They were 17 in number, aged between 4 and 7. He waited for the bus that was approaching to pass the first corner before he snapped his fingers. The bus lost control, and the children were still unaware. Zehra watched as demons took control of the situation. What followed was a disaster. Three children died instantly, and the rest scattered in fear. The boy whom the angels protected was shielded by their wings. He stared, paralyzed in fear. The bus swerved and knocked another boy unconscious, then landed on its back and exploded into flames; the fire killed nine children. Two others who were trying to escape were hit by another car that lost control.
Zehra watched, amazed. He had seen human life vanish in mere instants, but this was something else. This was a mindless massacre for entertainment. No wonder their father had made his judgment.

When the accident was over, people gathered, and weeping parents came to the scene along with security guards, then the police, and finally ambulances. The boy who had been saved had tears in his face. He watched as the bodies of his friends were wrapped in neat body bags. He did not even understand what was happening. Fear did not allow him. Their cries went up into the air. It was a series of questions he was used to hearing: Why God? Why did they have to die? Why me? Why me?
"Did you like the show?" He asked, joining him.
"It was too gruesome for my taste. I like to settle for a quiet death."
"Ever the diplomat. Don't worry, I do not intend to get you on God's bad side."
"What about the boy who was knocked unconscious?" Zehra asked.
"He will die tonight.” His countenance changed. “I've had my fun with him."
Zehra sighed and put his hands in his pockets. "Let us see the outcome of this game of yours."
"People are just that, Eva, people. Animals die without question; why should we be any different? We're the ones who feel entitled to living." Bryan argued.
"I don't know why you have such a masochistic view toward living.
You could do with more optimism."
"And more food," Matthew added.
They all laughed.

They had just closed from work and were sitting around the table in their booth. As always, Matthew was more focused on the meal than on the conversation. Eva, an unyielding optimist, was still bent on making Bryan see the good in every situation.He ate slowly, trying his best to be present in the moment. Still, he found himself drifting. He looked at the twirl of soup on Bryan’s plate and found his thoughts in turmoil.
"You have that look again," Eva said.
He snapped back and conjoined with his mechanical movements.
"What look?"
"You're lost in thought," she said. "Really, Zyair, if you keep this up, you will make your life much more complicated."
"Could it get any worse?" Matthew said.
"Seriously, Matthew?"
"It's not like the guy cares. He doesn't care about living; he doesn't see the use of being present in the moment. It couldn't be any worse than that."
"I'd try to be present. Sorry, I keep spacing out."
"What do you think about?" Eva asked as Matthew downed the last bit of his food.
"Too little of everything." He sighed and picked up his bag. "I've got to go. Tomorrow?"
"Running away again?" Matthew asked.
"I've got some..."
"Program I've got to attend to." They completed it together.
He smiled. "I see this excuse has gotten old. I'd look for what works."
“I may have some ideas,” Bryan said and waved.
Eva laughed. "Take care, Zyair."
"Later, buddy," Matthew added.

He waved and walked slowly. He drifted into his thoughts as soon as the door of the restaurant closed. He put on his headphones and slid his hands into his pockets. The night was chilly. You could catch your breath if you wanted to. He walked steadily, avoiding the road, making sure to look at the lights as he walked.

The sounds of blaring horns and speeding cars unnerved him. He almost always had a panic attack whenever he was out in public. He envied those who accepted automobiles as a part of society. He didn't feel threatened in one, but he rather stayed away from any as much as he could. He walked slowly, trying not to think. He looked back to make sure that a cyclist was not behind him. Sudden movements could unnerve you, and you could jump into the road. He wasn't scared of dying, but cars on the road scared him. Did that not mean that he was scared of dying? Dying was the final effect after all. It didn't matter what process it went with, dying was—
He bumped into a man and shrieked backward.
"I'm so sorry, sir. I'm so sorry. I would be more careful next time. I—"
"You don't have to be," the man said, picking up his phone that had fallen to the ground.
"What? No! I—"

"You were scared, I understand." The man placed his hand on his shoulder and came closer. His glasses reflected the moonlight. Zyair could not see his eyes properly. He was used to looking into people's eyes. You could tell a lot just by looking.
The man seemed to look over him. Zyair felt like he was standing in front of a tower. The man, who was a lot taller than he was, saw his disconcerted look and stepped back.
"You don't have to apologize for all of your mistakes. Some of them were not yours to begin with."
He kept silent and continued to stare.
"Perhaps, we might meet again sometime." The man said and smiled as he walked past.
"Yes, sir," Zyair replied, recovering himself as the man disappeared into the crowd.

He put his headphones back on and walked, more cautiously this time, closer to the shop windows. Where fewer people seemed to gather. He got to the front of the condo and looked around. His apartment was on the 11th floor. Something was strange today. He stared down the right side of the street. There were no lights, and it was unusually quiet. It was not just that. The security men who were supposed to be on guard were not in their posts. Those men never left their posts.
He decided to walk to the right side of the building. The closer he got, the darker it seemed to get until it was so dark he had to turn on the torchlight on his phone.

At first, nothing seemed unusual or out of place. It was just a dark alley with no sounds. But then he saw a trail of blood. He would have turned back, but he was curious. He knew that he should have been afraid, but what would he see? He went forward until he found Mr. Rogers on the ground, bleeding. He seemed to have been stabbed.
"Mr. Rogers!" He knelt beside him and was about to reach out when he thought otherwise. If Mr. Rogers died and they saw his prints, he would be a suspect.

"Mr. Rogers." He called, kneeling beside him. He felt a tightness in his chest. Death was everywhere around him. Today it was Mr. Rogers; tomorrow, it could be him. Eva would argue that it was wrong to think that way, but religious beliefs were an optimism that did not work well with life’s realism.
"Devils..." Mr. Rogers groaned.
"What?" He bent lower to hear what the man was saying.
"Devils..,” he said again.
"Devils?" Was the man delirious?
"Be careful." Mr. Rogers groaned.
Zyair dialed the emergency police contact available to the tenants of the condo and sent an anonymous tip about the incident. Mr. Rogers muttered something again.
He bent to listen closely. "Mr. Rogers, what was that?"
"They’re real, and they’re here... don’t let them get to it."
Zyair knew that Mr. Rogers had said his last words and had drawn his final breath.
He stared at the body in shock for a while and retreated from the scene with multiple reasons to be afraid before anyone would find him there.

chapters.label: Chapter 4
chapters.title: The Eleventh Hour
paras: She walked into the apartment and took a deep breath before looking around. She noticed the cozy living room with its comfortable sofa. She could imagine herself snuggling up there with a good book on a lazy afternoon. The large window caught her eye, and she imagined sitting there and looking out at the world outside. The kitchen had basic appliances, but she was happy to see that everything was clean and working. She pictured herself cooking a simple meal for herself or maybe inviting a friend over for a cozy dinner. Friends may come along the line, she comforted herself.

In the bedroom, she admired the simple but clean and comfortable bed. She noticed the dresser and closet and imagined herself putting her clothes away and making the space her own. She took note of the few decorative items, like the framed photo on the nightstand, and thought about what personal touches she could add to make the space her own. In the bathroom, she noticed the functional but clean space. She admired the shower/tub combo and the basic vanity with its mirror. She was pleased with the apartment. It may not be luxurious, but it had everything she needed to live comfortably. All that was left was moving her stuff in.

Zyair walked down the hallway of the apartment building; his attention was caught by the open door of the neighboring apartment. He paused in front of the door and glanced inside. There, he saw a young woman walking through the apartment, taking in the scenery. She seemed lost in thought and unaware of his presence. He was intrigued and wondered who this new neighbor might be. Mr. Rogers dies the night someone new moves directly opposite his apartment. It can't be a coincidence.

The young woman exuded a natural beauty that seemed to radiate from within. She stood with a confident and self-assured demeanor that would make her stand out in a crowd. She was wearing stylish clothing that flattered her figure without being too revealing, showcasing her impeccable taste.

The simple yet elegant blouse complemented her slender curves, paired with a fitted pair of pants that accentuated her long legs. Her clothing was tastefully accessorized with a delicate necklace and a pair of understated earrings, drawing attention to her striking features and highlighting her natural beauty.

As she moved through the apartment, her graceful movements caught his eye. She had her back turned to him, but he couldn't help but admire her effortless style, which perfectly complemented her stunning features. After taking the scene in, he slipped on his headphones and continued on his way, but he couldn't help feeling intrigued by her.
She turned when she heard a door snap shut. The man emerged from the room and adjusted his glasses.
"The bedroom could do with some pink paint." He smiled, "But I think everything else suits your taste."
"It will do." She nodded. "Who's the person in the other apartment?"
"Miss Lauren, I am a very busy man. If I knew everyone in my buildings, I might be forced to live in them rather than own them."
She kept silent, digesting his narcissism. "Thank you, sir," she replied after some seconds.
"Call me Dawn," he said.
He bowed at her as he walked out, closing the door behind him.

Genesys stood at the edge of the crowded street; a scowl etched deep into his features. He had just finished his shift at the local bookstore and was making his way home when he had the misfortune of crossing paths with a loudmouth who was spouting off opinions without any factual basis. He hated people like this. Arrogant worms who never morphed beyond the ignorance of their primal instincts.

Normally, Genesys would have just walked away, but he felt sympathy for the fools who hung around to listen. It was how society got rotten, fool by fool, and you had a useless generation on your hands. With fools being a constant threat to humanity, one would be grateful for plagues and their assistance in keeping the world's balance. He turned to face him, ready to engage in destructive psychoanalysis.
"You know, it's easy to spout off opinions," he began, his voice low and steady. "But it takes real intellect to back them up with actual facts and evidence."
The guy laughed, "Oh yeah? And what makes you say that, smarty pants? Do you think you’re smarter than I am?"

Genesys's scowl deepened as he stepped forward, his eyes narrowing in on his opponent. "As a matter of fact, yes, I am.” Let me ask you this," he said, his tone dripping with milky condescension. "Do you even know what it means to possess the ability for logical thought?"
The guy faltered, his eyes darting back and forth as he searched for an answer.
"Of course not. How could you? Because your brain is capable of some motor skills, you assume that you can think. You're a sad apology to average grade schoolers."
“Watch your tongue, mister, before I take that smugness off your face."

Genesys smirked and shook his head. Satisfied that he had put the arrogant fool in his place. He turned and continued down the street with the guy hurling insults at him, his mind already moving on to more important matters.

He continued walking, lost in thought. Lately, he had found himself thinking more and more about the value of life and its meaning. He couldn't help but wonder if life was really worth all the effort that went into living it or if it was some sad investment.

On the one hand, he understood the value of life. It was a precious thing, something to be cherished and protected. The struggle to live was the foundation of everything that was good in the world. Without it, there would be no love, no laughter, no joy. It was what gave meaning to everything else.

But on the other hand, he couldn't help but see the sheer worthlessness of life, as it was equally the cause of everything evil. People spent their entire lives chasing after things that ultimately didn't matter. They worked jobs they hated, spent time with people they didn't care about, and pursued empty dreams that would never come to fruition.

What was the point of all this effort, he wondered? Was life really worth it then, when it was just a never-ending cycle of pain and disappointment in a guild of values and principles? In a way, those who chose evil understood the world better.

As he walked, Genesys found himself getting lost in these thoughts. He wondered if there was more to life than just the pursuit of happiness. Maybe, he thought, there was a deeper purpose to it all, something that he had been missing all this time. Whatever the case, he knew one thing for sure. He was determined to find out the true value of life and to live it to the last of his terms, no matter what.

He climbed up the stairs and opened the door to his cramped apartment, feeling a sense of confinement wash over him. It was a small, single room that barely fit his bed, desk, and bookshelf. He couldn't help but feel like a bird in a cage, trapped and unable to spread his wings.

As he sat down on the bed and pulled off his shoes, Genesys pondered on his perspective that life was just a game to be played. It didn't matter if you won or lost; the real value was in knowing how to play. To him, it was nothing more than a series of moves on a giant chessboard, each one carefully calculated to give him an advantage.

Now he wondered if there was more to life than the play. Maybe, he thought, there was something deeper and more meaningful out there, something that he had been missing all this time. He had always prided himself on his morals and principles, but he couldn't help but wonder if the day would come when he would have the chance to put them to the test.
